summary:
I've been experimenting with SillyTavern character-creation tooling — specifically what it takes to build a character card that isn't just "generate fields from a prompt." I surveyed the existing extensions in that space first (there's really one incumbent, plus one much smaller project that independently converged on a similar phased design), and confirmed the gap: nobody does an interview-first flow where the tool asks you questions before any field exists, builds a persona, and generates art in the same loop. That's the niche I'm building into.

On the Japanese-learning side, I built a small coached dashboard for myself (稽古帳) rather than using Anki, because Anki's spaced-repetition model is a poor fit for kana — it optimizes for rare exposure, and kana needs automaticity instead. So I wrote a purpose-built drill: a placement pass, speed-gated recognition boxes, and a matching game that's explicitly an on-ramp and never counts as mastery. One redesign worth mentioning: the first version made you type romaji answers, and I stalled out three items in — typing forces you to produce a sound, which turned out to be testing a skill above what I'd actually learned yet. Switched it to tap-to-select with audio on every tile, and engagement picked right back up. That's usually the tell that a UI is testing the wrong thing.

For text-to-speech in that project I ended up on VOICEVOX over the more obvious Kokoro pick, because VOICEVOX exposes an editable two-stage API — you get back the reading and pitch accent before synthesis, and can patch a wrong mora before it ever becomes audio. Kokoro would've mispronounced certain characters (は as "wa" in isolation, silently, forever) with no way to fix it short of hacks. I added a build-time check that verifies every generated audio clip's reading against what was expected and fails the build on a mismatch — it's already caught two real errors before they shipped.

Smaller thing: I run a personal automation agent (Hermes-Agent) with a scheduler, and its cron jobs were setting a "this is an unattended job" flag on the whole process without ever clearing it — so once a day, right after the first scheduled job ran, every interactive command I sent it got silently treated as unattended and blocked. Took some log-diffing to catch since the failure mode looked unrelated to the cause. Fixed with a proper refcounted flag instead of a global on/off switch.

highlights.oneLiner: Building interview-first SillyTavern character creation into the unoccupied niche
